title: Ullambana
hook: the Chinese festival of offering for ancestors, from Moggallana's mother

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rains retreat: a vow of place, with a short leave for real need. Your line was stay in one place. Did you find the spot for this season's practice? Day one thousand four hundred seventeen.

Paper slips cover a long wall in a Chinese temple hall, row after row, each with a name brushed onto it. Some names belong to the dead: a grandfather, a mother, a baby who didn't live long. Some belong to the living: a sick father, a child taking exams. In front of the wall, tables are heaped with fruit, rice, flowers and cloth. Monks file in and chant. This is the Ullambana assembly, held in the seventh lunar month. You've met its Japanese cousin, Obon, with its fires and dances. Today stay in the Chinese hall, and look at why the wall holds the names of the living as well as the dead.
screen: `NAMES ON PAPER SLIPS.` → `THE DEAD AND THE LIVING.` → `WHY BOTH?`

segments.voice: First, the story, which the path told a few days ago at the home altar. In the Ullambana Sutra, a Chinese Buddhist scripture, the disciple Moggallana finds his dead mother among the hungry ghosts and can't feed her himself. The Buddha sends him to give, on the day the monks finish their summer retreat, to the whole community of monks: food, bowls, bedding, the things they need. Second, what the sutra does next, which is easy to miss. It doesn't stop with one mother. Moggallana asks whether other disciples, in times to come, could make the same offering for their own parents. The Buddha says yes, and widens it. Third, the living. The sutra doesn't only speak about the dead. It says the same offering helps parents who are still alive, bringing them long life and freedom from illness, and it reaches back through the generations of ancestors too. That's why the paper slips in the hall carry both kinds of names. Fourth, what the festival became. The sutra ends with the Buddha telling disciples who care for their parents to make this offering every year, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month. In China and across East Asia, families still bring names and offerings to temples in that month. Some readers hear in it a festival about care that runs both ways in time: for the parents who are still here, and the ones who came before them.
screen: `HE CAN'T FEED HER HIMSELF.` · `GIVE TO THE WHOLE COMMUNITY.` · `FOR THE LIVING AND THE DEAD.` · then, large: `FOR THE ANCESTORS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Now let one ancestor or parent come to mind, living or gone: a grandparent, a parent, someone you never met but carry the name of. If no one in your family feels right, a teacher or someone who raised you is fine. Picture their face, or just their name. Then think of one small thing you could offer in their name today, given to others rather than to them: a bag of groceries to a food bank, a donation, a meal for a neighbor, an hour of help. Choose it now. Then rest with them, and breathe, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Ullambana. The festival of offering for ancestors and living parents, from the story of Moggallana's mother. Today's word.
Your line: for the ancestors. Today, do the one thing you chose, and say their name quietly as you do it. Day one thousand four hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: In Chinese and other East Asian Buddhist communities, families bring offerings to temples in the seventh lunar month and register the names of deceased ancestors and living relatives, while monks chant the Ullambana assembly.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ullambana is a Chinese ghost festival.
what it means: an offering to the whole monastic community, made for parents living and dead, from the story of Moggallana's mother.
what a scholar hears: a scripture known in Chinese, whose title's Sanskrit origin scholars still debate, tying filial care to the end of the summer retreat.

notes: Ullambana Sutra paraphrased: Moggallana's food bursts into flame (not retold here); the Buddha says one person's power is not enough and directs offerings to the assembled sangha of the ten directions on the day they end the summer retreat (15th of the 7th month); the merit benefits present parents (long life, freedom from illness) and seven generations of ancestors. Confirm. The number of generations was left out of the voice per the claims rule.
